newsitem.title: USA: Stage is set for Hollywood's big Oscar night out.
newsitem.headline: Stage is set for Hollywood's big Oscar night out.

text.p: The stage was set, the red carpet was down and fans were camped out on Sunday ready for Hollywood's big night out -- the Academy Awards.

"I feel like a child, I am so excited," singer Celine Dion said, as she rehearsed at the Shrine Auditorium where Monday night she will sing one of the Oscar-nominated songs -- "Because You Loved Me," from the film "Up Close and Personal".

Comedian Billy Crystal, who will be back as host of the show after a three-year absence, said the Academy Awards show will be a three-hour test of his willpower not to say "Show me the money!" -- the overworked catch-phrase from Tom Cruise's nominated movie "Jerry Maguire".
"I'm trying to get through the show so I don't say it," Crystal told the Los Angeles Times.
As hairdressers and tuxedo rental stores were doing brisk business, Monday's Oscars show was embroiled in controversy. The focus was not on who would be at the ceremony, but, rather, who would not.
In an apparent snub to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, Barbra Streisand will not sing the Oscar-nominated song from "The Mirror Has Two Faces".
A spokeswoman for the academy told Reuters that Streisand pulled out and was not expected to attend. Natalie Cole will sing "I Finally Found Someone" instead.
Some news reports said Streisand was upset the film she directed and co-produced did not get a best picture nod.

Another no-show will be Hustler magazine publisher Larry Flynt, whose life was portrayed in the movie "The People vs Larry Flynt". He claimed Sony, the parent company of Columbia Pictures, did not invite him.

However, Flynt, who has been attacked as a pornographer by feminist groups, was at the Golden Globes award ceremony in January with actor Woody Harrelson, who played him in the film, and Courtney Love, who played his late wife Althea.
But for the Academy Awards, where Harrelson has been nominated for best actor and Milos Forman for best director, Columbia said it had no ticket for Flynt.
"The ironic thing about all this is that this film is about censorship," Flynt told the Los Angeles Times.
Unfazed, about 1,000 fans -- some had been waiting since Wednesday -- were camped out on bleachers at the arrivals area outside the Shrine Auditorium.
In a year with few big-name stars nominated, competition appeared to be wide open. The only Oscar certainty seemed to be Lauren Bacall as best supporting actress for "The Mirror Has Two Faces".
Much like Paul Newman's best actor Oscar in 1986 for "The Colour of Money", Bacall was a sentimental favourite to win as a reward for 50 years in Hollywood without a nomination.

The buzz in Hollywood this year? According to the Los Angeles Times, there is no buzz. "Maybe it's because the people up for awards don't have a lot of enemies or friends in this town," one producer told the newspaper.
Indeed, in the major categories, only Cruise -- best actor nominee for "Jerry Maguire" and Diane Keaton, best actress nominee for "Marvin's Room" -- are A-list stars.
Harrelson, Ralph Fiennes (best actor for "The English Patient") and James Woods (best supporting actor for "Ghosts of Mississippi") are B-list performers, but the rest?

The average movie fan would be hard-pressed to identify Brenda Blethyn ("Secrets & Lies"), Frances McDormand ("Fargo"), Kristin Scott Thomas ("The English Patient") or Emily Watson ("Breaking the Waves") as best actress.
For best actor, neither Billy Bob Thornton ("Sling Blade") nor Geoffrey Rush ("Shine") are household names.
The supporting actor category is completed by first-time nominees, Cuba Gooding Jr. ("Jerry Maguire"), William Macy ("Fargo"), Armin Mueller-Stahl ("Shine") and Edward Norton ("Primal Fear").

Besides Bacall, the supporting actress group has Joan Allen ("The Crucible"), who was nominated last year for "Nixon", and Barbara Hershey ("The Portrait of a Lady"), who is certainly a recognisable actress.
But Juliette Binoche ("The English Patient") and Marianne Jean-Baptiste ("Secrets & Lies") are unknowns.

If precedents mean anything, then "The English Patient", which picked up 12 nominations, had a good chance of winning best picture. In the last 25 years, the film with the most nominations won the best picture Oscar 21 times.
Director Anthony Minghella said the film "treats audiences as grown-ups -- it asks them to think and feel."
The five nominations for best foreign film are: "A Chef in Love" (Georgia), "Kolya" (Czech Republic), "The Other Side of Sunday (Norway), "Prisoner of the Mountains" (Russia) and "Ridicule" (France).
